newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY POLICE SAY THEY POWERLESS AS GANG WAR GROWS.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY POLICE SAY THEY POWERLESS AS GANG WAR GROWS.

text.p: Hungarian police said on Tuesday they were making little headway against a mushrooming gang war whose latest target was a luxury car dealership attacked with hand grenades.
"The entire organised crime staff of the Budapest police is working on the bombing series, but we are short of manpower," Hungarian police spokesman Mihaily Deszi told Reuters.
Hungary's new national police chief, Attila Berta, told Hungarian radio he expects further attacks linked to what he called a "mafia war associated with the development of society".
At least three people have been killed and almost two dozen car showrooms, restaurants, pubs, nightclubs or peep shows have been damaged since September by hand grenades or petrol-filled bombs.
Residents of the city of two million people are becoming alarmed by the rash of attacks which has escalated in recent weeks.
Hand grenades thrown over a chain-link fence into the outdoor lot of the Auto Super dealership in the capital seriously damaged one car and caused minor damage to several others, police said.
They said witnesses saw one or two men running away after the attack on Monday night.
It was the fourth attack in less than a week, including a hand grenade bombing in the toilet of a Chinese restaurant on Friday which killed the owner's wife and daughter.

Diplomats said the attacks, such as the one at the Chinese restaurant and a petrol-bombing on Monday morning of a Greek-owned club which specialised in American country music, were getting closer to hitting tourist locations.
"It's one thing when they attack a peep show, it's another when it's a mainstream restaurant," one diplomat said.
"I don't think it's there yet (affecting the tourist industry) but it could have a chilling effect."
Police have made few arrests and say they have received little cooperation from victims.
The owner of the car dealership, an Afghani national who is a naturalised Hungarian, declined to tell reporters his name and added, "I don't know anything about this."
Other countries in eastern Europe have been hit by an upsurge in crime since the collapse of communism in 1989.
Violent crime has soared in Bulgaria and is worsening with the country's economic collapse. Car bombs are a popular way of settling scores between powerful mafia-type business groups.

In the latest such attack, a former military prosecutor and his wife were badly injured on Monday when a bomb wrecked their car outside their home in the Bulgarian capital Sofia. General Lilko Yotsov worked as an adviser to such a business group after retiring.
Political analysts said societies in transition may experience an upsurge in crime, but it is not an excuse for the authorities to throw up their hands in despair.

"If it is the natural consequence (of change), I think if sociologists or political scientists say it that is one thing but if the police chief is going to use that argument it is just not right," said Istvan Stumpf of the Budapest School of Politics.
